corrections.notes: MERINO (JAMA 2018) did not show non-inferiority: 30-day mortality was 12.3% with pip-tazo vs 3.7% with meropenem. A carbapenem remains preferred definitive therapy for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli/Klebsiella BSI (IDSA AMR guidance).
corrections.source: MERINO trial (Harris et al, JAMA 2018); IDSA Guidance on treatment of antimicrobial-resistant Gram-negative infections (2024)
corrections.newExplanation: Ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli in the blood usually means an ESBL producer. In the MERINO trial, piperacillin-tazobactam failed to show non-inferiority to meropenem: 30-day mortality was 12.3% vs 3.7%. IDSA 2024 guidance therefore recommends a carbapenem, such as meropenem, as definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection, even if the isolate tests susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam. Cefepime and aztreonam are not reliable options. Source: MERINO trial (Harris et al, JAMA 2018); IDSA Guidance on treatment of antimicrobial-resistant Gram-negative infections (2024)

corrections.notes: RCOphth 2022 RVO guidance doesn't recommend thrombophilia screening when conventional vascular risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidaemia) explain the occlusion in an older patient; testing is reserved for young patients without risk factors, bilateral RVO or thrombosis history.
corrections.source: RCOphth Clinical Guidelines: Retinal Vein Occlusion (2022); BSH guideline on testing for heritable thrombophilia (Arachchillage et al, 2022)
corrections.newExplanation: In an older patient, retinal vein occlusion is mainly driven by conventional vascular risk factors such as hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes and glaucoma. RCOphth guidance does not recommend routine thrombophilia screening in this group. Testing is reserved for younger patients (under about 50), bilateral or recurrent occlusion, or a personal or family history of thrombosis. BSH 2022 also advises against untargeted heritable thrombophilia testing, because results rarely change management. Source: RCOphth Clinical Guidelines: Retinal Vein Occlusion (2022); BSH guideline on testing for heritable thrombophilia (Arachchillage et al, 2022)

A 38-year-old with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes should therefore have statins discussed and considered now, not deferred to age 40. Source: NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification (2023); NICE NG17 Type 1 diabetes in adults

corrections.notes: Confusion, asterixis and myoclonus in a haemodialysis patient suggest uraemic (or drug-related) encephalopathy. The critical step is to optimise or intensify dialysis after excluding other causes, not to request a neurology consult.
corrections.source: Brouns R, De Deyn PP. Neurological complications in renal failure: a review. Clin Neurol Neurosurg 2004; Lacerda G et al. Neurological complications of renal failure. Pract Neurol 2010
corrections.newExplanation: New confusion, asterixis and myoclonus in a patient on haemodialysis point to uraemic encephalopathy from inadequate dialysis. Accumulated renally cleared drugs, such as gabapentinoids, opioids or cefepime, can cause a similar picture. After checking for hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, infection and drug toxicity, the key step is to intensify dialysis, which usually reverses the encephalopathy. Neurology input can help if the picture is atypical, but it should not delay dialysis. Source: Brouns R, De Deyn PP. Neurological complications in renal failure: a review. Clin Neurol Neurosurg 2004; Lacerda G et al. Neurological complications of renal failure. Pract Neurol 2010

corrections.notes: Homocysteine is raised in both folate and B12 deficiency, so it doesn't distinguish them. In megaloblastic anaemia, a normal serum cobalamin (with raised homocysteine but normal MMA) is what points to folate deficiency.
corrections.source: BSH guideline for diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders (Devalia et al, Br J Haematol 2014)
corrections.newExplanation: Folate and cobalamin deficiency both cause megaloblastic anaemia and both raise homocysteine, so a raised homocysteine cannot tell them apart. Methylmalonic acid rises only in B12 deficiency, and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies point to pernicious anaemia. In a patient with megaloblastic anaemia, a normal serum cobalamin (ideally with a normal MMA) is what directs you towards folate deficiency, which is then confirmed with serum or red-cell folate. Source: BSH guideline for diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders (Devalia et al, Br J Haematol 2014)

corrections.notes: BSG (Gut 2010), ASGE and the AGA 2025 polyp update advise removing hyperplastic polyps over 1 cm because of dysplasia/neoplasia risk, and testing for and eradicating H. pylori. A 1.2 cm hyperplastic polyp should be resected, not left with 5-year follow-up.
corrections.source: BSG guidelines for the management of gastric polyps (Goddard et al, Gut 2010); AGA Clinical Practice Update on management of gastric polyps (2025)
corrections.newExplanation: Gastric hyperplastic polyps carry a small risk of dysplasia and carcinoma, and the risk rises with size. BSG and AGA guidance advise endoscopic removal of hyperplastic polyps larger than 1 cm, or those that are pedunculated or symptomatic. The surrounding mucosa should be biopsied, and H. pylori should be tested for and eradicated if present. A 1.2 cm hyperplastic polyp should therefore be resected, for example by EMR or snare polypectomy, rather than left with only distant follow-up. Source: BSG guidelines for the management of gastric polyps (Goddard et al, Gut 2010); AGA Clinical Practice Update on management of gastric polyps (2025)

corrections.notes: For uncomplicated GERD with sustained symptom control, AGA (2022 deprescribing update), ACG 2022 and NICE CG184 advise trying step-down or discontinuation (or on-demand use), with warning about rebound symptoms. Indefinite continuation is for complicated disease (severe oesophagitis, Barrett's).
corrections.source: AGA Clinical Practice Update on deprescribing of proton pump inhibitors (Targownik et al, Gastroenterology 2022); NICE CG184 Dyspepsia and GORD
corrections.newExplanation: Patients with uncomplicated GERD whose symptoms are fully controlled should be offered an attempt to step down or stop PPI therapy, or to switch to on-demand use. Warn them that rebound acid hypersecretion can cause temporary symptoms, which can be managed by tapering. Long-term continuous PPI is recommended for complicated disease, such as severe (LA grade C/D) oesophagitis, Barrett's oesophagus or peptic stricture, none of which applies here. pH testing is not needed before a trial off treatment. Source: AGA Clinical Practice Update on deprescribing of proton pump inhibitors (Targownik et al, Gastroenterology 2022); NICE CG184 Dyspepsia and GORD
